notes.bp: An ASR training set should cover acoustic diversity and should spend labeling effort where the transcription is uncertain.
notes.wh: Random sampling can overrepresent easy or similar speech, while uncertainty-only sampling can repeat rare errors without broad acoustic coverage.
notes.naive: Sample randomly, or rank clips by model uncertainty alone and call the resulting set diverse.
notes.ap: Combine acoustic-diversity measures with transcription uncertainty when selecting training data, then test the effect on ASR.
notes.mech: The paper proposes hybrid data sampling for ASR by integrating acoustic diversity and transcription uncertainty.
notes.math: Data selection is a coverage-allocation problem: diversity broadens the conditions seen, while uncertainty targets the model's unresolved boundary.
notes.ww: The paper reports ASR improvements from hybrid sampling relative to the tested selection strategies.
notes.limits: Acoustic representation, uncertainty estimator, corpus, budget, language, and split bound the result; a sampling score is not a complete measure of data value.
notes.title: Hybrid Data Sampling for ASR: Integrating Acoustic Diversity and Transcription Uncertainty

notes.bp: A speech-to-speech language model in a duplex conversation must listen and speak at overlapping times without losing the current turn or waiting for a full utterance.
notes.wh: Duplex interaction couples streaming recognition, generation, interruption, and turn timing; a model optimized for one direction can block or talk over the other.
notes.naive: Use a turn-taking pipeline that waits for end-of-speech or run separate listen and speak models with no shared state.
notes.ap: Build an efficient direct duplex model that represents incoming and outgoing speech jointly and evaluates real-time speech-to-speech behavior.
notes.mech: The paper studies efficient and direct duplex modeling for speech-to-speech language models.
notes.math: Duplexity is a control problem over concurrent streams: the model must decide what to retain, when to respond, and when to yield while generating speech.
notes.ww: The paper reports efficiency and interactive speech-to-speech results for the duplex model.
notes.limits: Latency, overlap, interruptions, model size, dialogue tasks, and evaluation protocol bound the result; a real-time demo is not robust open-ended conversation.
notes.title: Efficient and Direct Duplex Modeling for Speech-to-Speech Language Model

notes.bp: A speech deepfake detector should generalize to unseen generators and conditions rather than becoming sharp only on the training attacks.
notes.wh: Sharp decision boundaries can fit artifacts specific to known generators; improving training fit may reduce performance when the attack distribution changes.
notes.naive: Optimize closed-set accuracy and assume a sharper classifier is more discriminative under every attack.
notes.ap: Study how sharpness relates to deepfake-detector generalization and use training changes that improve the boundary's transfer to unseen attacks.
notes.mech: The paper studies moving from sharpness to better generalization for speech deepfake detection.
notes.math: Generalization depends on the geometry of the learned boundary, not just its training margin; the relevant test is behavior on new attack sources.
notes.ww: The paper reports deepfake-detection generalization results linked to sharpness and the proposed training approach.
notes.limits: Attack types, datasets, sharpness measure, training recipe, and open-set split bound the claim; no benchmark proves future attack coverage.
notes.title: From Sharpness to Better Generalization for Speech Deepfake Detection

notes.bp: Speakers with different articulatory habits can produce similar apical vowels, but the physical movements behind those sounds may differ across Southwestern Mandarin speakers.
notes.wh: Tongue shape, place, and coarticulation interact, and acoustic similarity hides multiple articulatory solutions.
notes.naive: Describe the vowel only by formants or assume one acoustic target has one tongue configuration.
notes.ap: Measure articulatory variation in apical vowels and relate it to acoustic outcomes across Southwestern Mandarin speakers.
notes.mech: The paper analyzes articulatory variations in apical vowels in Southwestern Mandarin.
notes.math: The sound-to-movement mapping is underdetermined: production data reveal which physical differences are tolerated while the acoustic category stays recognizable.
notes.ww: The paper reports articulatory variation and its acoustic relationships for the studied apical vowels.
notes.limits: Speakers, dialect region, imaging or measurement method, vowel context, and sample size limit generalization; variation is not pathology.
notes.title: Articulatory variations in Apical Vowels in Southwestern Mandarin

notes.bp: When editing text-based speech, changing a word should preserve the intended emotion and keep the new audio emotionally consistent with its context.
notes.wh: Text edits can alter sentiment, emphasis, and prosody at once; a locally fluent replacement may sound emotionally wrong next to surrounding speech.
notes.naive: Replace the text and synthesize the whole sentence, or optimize word correctness without an emotion-consistency check.
notes.ap: Create an emotion-consistent speech-editing task and model that preserves affect across the edited span and its context.
notes.mech: EmoCorrector and the ECD-TSE dataset target emotionally consistent text-based speech editing.
notes.math: Editing has two invariants: linguistic content must change as requested, while speaker identity and emotional trajectory must remain coherent around the change.
notes.ww: The paper reports dataset and model results for emotionally consistent speech editing.
notes.limits: Emotion labels, edit types, speakers, context, synthesis model, and perceptual evaluation bound the claim; emotional consistency is listener- and culture-dependent.
notes.title: Towards Emotionally Consistent Text-Based Speech Editing: Introducing EmoCorrector and The ECD-TSE Dataset

notes.bp: A bandwidth-limited recording can sound muffled; a bandwidth-extension model should restore useful high-frequency detail without inventing harsh or speaker-inconsistent content.
notes.wh: The missing band is not uniquely determined by the low band, and waveform metrics may reward artifacts that listeners dislike.
notes.naive: Copy the low-band waveform or add fixed high-frequency noise and assume the result is natural.
notes.ap: Use a hybrid waveform bandwidth-extension network and evaluate reconstruction quality, speech content, and perceptual naturalness.
notes.mech: HWB-Net is a high-performance efficient hybrid waveform bandwidth-extension method.
notes.math: Bandwidth extension is constrained synthesis: the model predicts plausible missing detail from the observed signal while preserving timing and identity in the known band.
notes.ww: The paper reports quality and efficiency results for HWB-Net on bandwidth-extension tests.
notes.limits: Bandwidth limit, speakers, noise, training targets, metrics, and listening protocol bound the result; plausible detail is not recovered ground truth.
notes.title: HWB-Net: A Novel High-Performance and Efficient Hybrid Waveform Bandwidth Extension Method

notes.bp: A multilingual speech synthesizer needs token units that can be shared across languages while still preserving language-specific pronunciation and rhythm.
notes.wh: Separate vocabularies waste capacity, while a universal token can erase distinctions or make the language model confuse languages.
notes.naive: Train one token set per language or force all languages into a text-like universal code without testing interference.
notes.ap: Learn a language-independent speech token and use it with language-model synthesis across multiple languages.
notes.mech: LIST is a language-independent speech token for multilingual speech synthesis with language models.
notes.math: The token is a cross-language interface: shared units carry reusable speech structure, while language conditioning reconstructs the differences needed for intelligible output.
notes.ww: The paper reports multilingual synthesis quality and cross-language token behavior for LIST.
notes.limits: Languages, token rate, codebook, speakers, conditioning, and evaluation metrics bound the claim; shared tokens do not guarantee equal quality.
notes.title: LIST: Language-Independent Speech Token for Multilingual Speech Synthesis with Language Models

notes.bp: An embodied conversational agent should adapt its spoken response to what a person says, sees, and does while the interaction is happening.
notes.wh: Multimodal inputs arrive at different times and the agent must keep a coherent conversational state while meeting real-time limits.
notes.naive: Fuse all sensors once per turn or use a scripted avatar with fixed responses and call it adaptive.
notes.ap: Build a general-purpose real-time multimodal embodied-agent framework that updates perception, dialogue, action, and speech together.
notes.mech: GenECA is a framework for real-time adaptive multimodal embodied conversational agents.
notes.math: Embodied conversation is a closed loop: perception changes the state, the state selects language and action, and the agent's output changes the next observation.
notes.ww: The paper reports real-time adaptive-agent behavior across its tested multimodal interaction settings.
notes.limits: Sensors, embodiment, latency, dialogue tasks, user studies, and policy constraints bound the claim; a framework demonstration is not human-level social understanding.
notes.title: GenECA: A General-Purpose Framework for Real-Time Adaptive Multimodal Embodied Conversational Agents
